notes: Professionalism legal from 20 July 1885; a professional registers with the FA (docs/data/history/RECRUITMENT_1888-1900.md §3).

Born within 6 miles of the ground or lived there 2 years. Dropped in 1889 (Inglis 1988, cited by the Wikipedia overview; month unknown). Whether it applied only to Cup ties is not confirmed. Clubs met it by having a signing 'take up his residence near the ground' (Lancashire Evening Post, 25 Aug 1888).
A professional may not play for more than one club in a season without special permission.

sources: Lancashire Evening Post, 25 Aug 1888 (period press, transcribed at https://bluecorrespondent.co.uk/1888-89/august1888.html)
notes: 'No player shall sign a second registration paper in one season without the consent of the Council.' `pence` = the retaining fees Everton repaid for Ross (£17 10s), an example of what the old club may claim. The text is a period newspaper read through a fan transcription (non-commercial: cross-check pending), so medium.

Sunderland lost 2 points (Sep 1890) for playing Doig before his League registration had run 7 days. Wikipedia gives the deduction; the 7-day length comes from LFChistory (non-commercial, not yet cross-checked). The earliest sourced date of the rule, not its start.
The SFA barred known professionals (men paid to play in England) until professionalism was legalised in Scotland in 1893 (560 registered).

From 1893-94 a League club keeps a player's registration after his contract ends; another club needs its consent and pays a fee. Before this, players moved freely between seasons (a 1891 start is not supported).

Maximum wage £4 a week (960 pence), bonuses banned. Sources differ between 1900 and 1901 for the FA decision. A claimed 1893 cap (£140 a year) may have been a proposal only and is not used. The £10 signing-on limit has no sourced date yet (gap).
